filmIssues: The rise separates the swimmer from the white splash that belongs with him: the splash stays on the clean background while the cut-out lifts and grows, so by t=0.6-1 the burst reads detached around his waist.

A visible ghost is revealed in the blue water below the swimmer as he moves up and scales to 1.12 — dark black shards/fragments appear in the waves at the spot he vacated, clearest in the bottom row of frames.

The final frame is over-tight rather than triumphant: the swimmer balloons toward the scoreboard, his hands crowd the black board and the composition loses the pool, lane ropes and stadium context that make the win read. The opening at zoom 1.05 is also already cropped in, so the move is mostly a plain push-in plus layer growth.

The light-sweep is not objectionable and suits a gold-medal moment, but it does not compensate for the splash/ghost separation; overall the film is only a little above a centred push-in in storytelling clarity.

plan.rationale: A triumph — Singapore's first Olympic gold — told as a rise: the swimmer lifts and grows while the camera tilts up and closes in, lifting his raised arms toward the scoreboard above the pool.

filmIssues: The film is essentially a plain centred push-in: a slow zoom from 1 to 1.28 with a small upward pan and almost no independent swimmer movement. It reads clearly, but it does not visibly enact the victory beyond what the baseline push-in would do.

The swimmer's own drift (-0.018) and scale (1.05) at depth 0.6 are so reduced that in the contact sheet he appears locked to the background; there is no clear rise, surge, or celebratory lift separating the hero from the splash and pool.

First frame is a good true wide opening (scoreboard, lights, lane ropes and pool all readable) and the last frame is a usable heroic hold, with no obvious tearing, doubled edges, halo, ghosting, or awkward frame-edge clipping in the six frames. Coherence is therefore not the problem — timidity is.
The light-sweep ambient is fitting for stadium triumph and is subtle enough not to disturb the cut-paper print style, but it is not visible enough in the stills to carry the story on its own.

rounds.verdict: The plate is clean — the swimmer is correctly shown from behind as a silhouette, anatomy and hands read well, the scoreboard is blank with no stray text or numbers, and the cut-paper style fits the contemporary print brief — but the film withholds its subject at the open and then pulls him away from his splash.
filmIssues: The first frame is a failed opening picture: the rise entrance means t=0 shows the splash and pool with no swimmer at all, so the page opens on an empty scene.
The swimmer's rise separates him from the splash that belongs with him. The white splash stays on the background while the body lifts away from it, tearing the cut-paper subject apart.

As the swimmer rises, the painted-over area behind him is revealed as a visible ghost — lane ropes and splash remnants in the clean background read across/behind the moving figure and make the separation obvious.

By t=1 the exaggerated combined rise, 1.12 scale, 0.85 depth and 1.38 camera push carry his raised hands into the bottom edge of the scoreboard. The final dwell frame feels over-cropped and awkward rather than triumphant, and the triumph gesture collides with the scoreboard instead of sitting under it.

The light-sweep is subtle and era-appropriate, but it cannot compensate for the missing opening subject and the splash/body separation. Overall the move is no better than — and less coherent than — a plain centred push-in.

plan.rationale: Make the triumph a visible rise, not just a push-in: open wide and slightly low on the full stadium, then have the swimmer rise early (enter rise 0-0.45) and continue drifting up -0.045 with growth to 1.12 at higher depth 0.85 so he surges out of the splash with real parallax against the scoreboard and lane ropes.
